newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-SCHALKE CELEBRATE COMPUTER-AIDED WIN OVER MILAN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SCHALKE CELEBRATE COMPUTER-AIDED WIN OVER MILAN.

text.p: A laptop computer filled with the penalty-kicking habits of Inter Milan's high-priced stars helped underdogs Schalke to their improbable UEFA Cup triumph on Wednesday.

Schalke goalkeeper Jens Lehmann and captain Olaf Thon revealed on Thursday the team had studied the computer records prepared by coach Huub Stevens, scouring the data for useful clues on who kicks where under what conditions.
The data helped Lehmann stop Inter's crucial first penalty kick by Ivan Zamorano and paved the way for the 4-1 penalty shoot-out win over the favourites.
"I had checked with the laptop and whenever Zamorano took a long run up he always kicked it to the (goalkeeper's) left," Lehmann said. "And that's exactly what he did."
Lehmann's diving save of Zamorano's shot put immense pressure on Inter, whose fate was then sealed moments later when Aron Winter sidefooted his spot-kick wide of the goal.

"Huub Stevens had all the Inter players and their preferred corners stored in the computer," Thon confirmed. "What also helped us is that Inter's goalie (Gianluca) Pagliuca kept deciding a bit too early which corner he was going to defend."
Schalke scored all four of their penalties for the win, which touched off an all-night celebration in the Ruhr Valley city of Gelsenkirchen.
A crowd of 60,000 met the team for another celebration at the town hall in the early afternoon.
"The next few days are going to filled with drink," said striker Martin Max.
"It will take a while for it to sink in that we have achieved the greatest win in club history," said Thon.
The city of 300,000, 150 km (90 miles) north of Bonn, is best known for grimy smokestacks and high unemployment. One in three families relies on jobless benefits.
Undeterred by steady rainfall, more than 30,000 Schalke fans watched the match on a giant video screen at the team's Park Stadium and city streets were almost deserted during the match.
It was the first European trophy in Schalke's 93-year history and their first title of any kind in 25 years.
"You simply cannot imagine what the success of Schalke means for this whole region," said Andre Mueller, a local priest.
"Schalke is a whole way of life for everyone here. A lot of people say they feel like second class Germans. This has elevated their self-worth to an astonishing degree."
He said he wasn't able to sleep more than an hour because there was so much celebratory noise in the city. He said many schools cancelled classes because no one was in a learning mood on Thursday.
"We are invincible," one Schalke fan shouted.
Schalke are in 12th place in the 18-team Bundesliga and, despite having the most rabidly faithful fans in the country, had long failed to fulfil their potential.

Thousands of honking cars came to a standstill in the centre of Gelsenkirchen, where unemployment is more than 20 percent, and many excited fans danced in the streets. Police said the celebrations lasted until around 5 a.m.
Several thousand fans then made their way to the local airport to meet the team, which landed at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT).
Two planned low-altitude "victory laps" around the city by the plane's pilot were dropped because so many fans were waiting to greet the team.
Schalke captured their last major trophy in 1972 when they won the German Cup.
